meta.reviewStatus: Draft translations of draft educational guides — have them reviewed by a healthcare professional before publication.

translations.title: Hashimoto’s and hypothyroidism: what’s the difference?
translations.summary: Two closely related ideas that are not the same thing. Here are the essentials to better understand your journey.
translations.intro: The thyroid produces hormones that help regulate many of the body’s functions. Hashimoto’s and hypothyroidism are linked, but they do not mean the same thing.

sections.heading: Hashimoto’s, an autoimmune disease
sections.body: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is a condition in which the immune system attacks the thyroid. It can gradually reduce the thyroid’s ability to produce hormones, but how it evolves varies from person to person.

sections.heading: Hypothyroidism, an underactive thyroid
sections.body: Hypothyroidism means the thyroid does not provide enough hormones for the body’s needs. It can have several causes, Hashimoto’s being one of them.

sections.heading: Symptoms alone are not enough to conclude
sections.body: Tiredness, feeling cold or difficulty concentrating can have many causes. Diagnosis and follow-up rely on a medical assessment and on tests suited to your situation.

sections.heading: Monitoring suited to you
sections.body: You can have Hashimoto’s while your thyroid still makes enough hormones. Your doctor may then monitor how it works with tests chosen for your situation. Ask which results are followed, when to repeat the tests and which changes mean you should get back in touch.

takeaways: Hashimoto’s is an autoimmune disease; hypothyroidism describes a lack of thyroid hormones.
Hashimoto’s does not always cause hypothyroidism straight away.
Only a healthcare professional can interpret your results in context.

translations.title: TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies: what are these tests looking for?
translations.summary: These antibodies can help look for an autoimmune cause; on their own, they do not tell the whole story about your thyroid.
translations.intro: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies and thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies are markers your doctor may request in some situations. They are not the same as TRAb, covered in the guide on Graves’ disease.

sections.heading: What do the abbreviations mean?
sections.body: Anti-TPO antibodies target thyroid peroxidase, and anti-Tg antibodies target thyroglobulin, two components involved in how the thyroid works. A doctor may test for them when looking for an autoimmune cause of a thyroid problem.

sections.heading: Does a positive result give the full answer?
sections.body: No. The result is read alongside TSH, sometimes free T4 (FT4), your symptoms and the rest of your medical history. Having antibodies does not, on its own, show whether treatment is needed.

sections.heading: Why are these tests not always done?
sections.body: Which test is ordered depends on the medical question. A doctor may check TPO antibodies first and, in some situations, thyroglobulin antibodies. Ask what the result is meant to clarify in your case.

takeaways: TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies are different from TRAb.
An antibody result is not interpreted on its own.
Your doctor chooses which tests to order based on the context.

translations.title: TSH, FT4, FT3: what the abbreviations mean
translations.summary: These markers have different roles. Find out what they are for and why they are read together.
translations.intro: Thyroid tests help healthcare professionals assess how the thyroid is working. How they are interpreted depends on the context, the treatment and the laboratory’s reference ranges.

sections.heading: TSH
sections.body: Produced by the pituitary gland, TSH helps regulate the production of thyroid hormones. It is often used to screen for and monitor hypothyroidism.

sections.heading: Free T4 (FT4)
sections.body: T4 is a hormone produced by the thyroid. The free fraction is the part that is not bound to transport proteins.

sections.heading: Free T3 (FT3)
sections.body: T3 is a biologically active thyroid hormone. It is not needed in every assessment of hypothyroidism.

takeaways: A single figure does not allow you to draw every conclusion.
Compare results using the units and reference ranges given by the laboratory.
Do not change your treatment based on a guide or on a single result.

translations.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism: understanding a borderline result
translations.summary: A TSH above the reference range with FT4 within its range is not always enough to decide on treatment.
translations.intro: “Subclinical hypothyroidism” describes a particular pattern of blood test results. How it is interpreted depends on the results, how they change over time, your symptoms and your medical situation. This guide cannot be used to diagnose anything from your own result.

sections.heading: What does “subclinical” mean?
sections.body: The term usually describes a TSH above the reference range while free T4 (FT4) stays within the laboratory’s range. Your doctor checks the context and may suggest a repeat test before drawing a conclusion.

sections.heading: Treatment is not automatic
sections.body: The decision takes several things into account: repeated results, symptoms, age, medical history and other health factors. A single value cannot show whether treatment is needed.

sections.heading: Questions to ask
sections.body: Ask whether the result should be repeated, what is being taken into account and when to get back in touch. Do not try to correct a result yourself by changing a medicine or taking a supplement.

takeaways: A TSH above the range with a normal FT4 does not, on its own, tell the whole story.
The context, and repeated results where needed, matter.
The decision to treat or to monitor is made with your healthcare professional.

translations.title: TSH and age: why context matters
translations.summary: How a TSH result is read depends on your age, your symptoms and your medical situation.
translations.intro: TSH is a marker used to assess the thyroid. In older people, reading it calls for particular care. A single result is not enough, on its own, to decide that treatment is needed.

sections.heading: Symptoms that are less specific
sections.body: Tiredness, slowing down or difficulty concentrating can have several explanations, especially with age. Your doctor takes into account all your symptoms, your medical history and your treatments.

sections.heading: A result read with age in mind
sections.body: With age, a TSH result may be read differently than in a younger adult. Your doctor considers it alongside your other results, other health conditions and some medicines: the decision is not simply a matter of comparing a number with a range found online.

sections.heading: Questions to ask
sections.body: Ask what the result means in your situation, whether a repeat test is useful and which changes you should report. Do not start, stop or change a treatment without medical advice.

takeaways: Age is part of the context for interpreting TSH.
A single symptom or a single value is not enough to draw a conclusion.
Decisions about follow-up or treatment are for your healthcare professional.

translations.title: Thyroid blood tests: before and after
translations.summary: A few checks before the test, then a careful look at the report, make it easier to discuss the results with your doctor.
translations.intro: Instructions can vary depending on the tests ordered and your situation. Before the test, check what the laboratory asks of you; afterwards, read each result with its unit and reference range, without drawing conclusions on your own.

sections.heading: Check the instructions
sections.body: Look at the request form and the laboratory’s information. Do not assume you need to fast: follow the instructions given for the tests actually ordered, and ask the person who ordered them what to do with your medicines on the day.

sections.heading: Mention your medicines and supplements
sections.body: Tell the professional who orders the test, and the team taking the sample, about your medicines, vitamins and supplements. Do not stop a treatment on your own initiative.

sections.heading: Reading the report
sections.body: Find the name of the test, the result, its unit and the reference range given by the laboratory. These help you read the report, but they are not enough to make a diagnosis. Different methods can give slightly different values.

sections.heading: Compare with care
sections.body: To follow changes over time, take into account the dates, your treatment and any change of laboratory. A value within the range does not always answer every question, and a value outside it does not explain the cause on its own. Ask your doctor what the result means for you.

takeaways: Follow the laboratory’s and your prescriber’s instructions, without assuming you need to fast.
Read each result together with its unit and the laboratory’s reference range.
Do not change a treatment based on a single number.

translations.title: Biotin and blood tests: remember to mention your supplements
translations.summary: Biotin can interfere with some laboratory tests: tell your doctor and the laboratory about any supplements you take.
translations.intro: Biotin, also called vitamin B7, is found in some supplements, especially those sold for hair or nails. Depending on the method used, it can interfere with some laboratory tests. Do not change how you take a supplement without asking for advice.

sections.heading: Why mention it?
sections.body: Biotin can make some laboratory results falsely high or falsely low. The effect depends on the test and the method used: it does not affect every test or every laboratory.

sections.heading: What to do before a blood test
sections.body: Tell the doctor who ordered the test, and the laboratory team, about all the supplements and medicines you take, including those bought without a prescription. Follow their instructions for your test.

sections.heading: Should you stop taking biotin?
sections.body: Do not stop it or change when you take it on your own initiative. Your doctor or the laboratory will tell you whether any precaution is needed for the planned test.

takeaways: Mention supplements containing biotin before a blood test.
Interference depends on the test and the laboratory’s method.
Do not stop a supplement without advice from a professional.

sources.label: FDA — Biotin interference with laboratory tests

translations.title: Taking levothyroxine properly
translations.summary: How you take your treatment can affect how well it is absorbed. A few useful everyday pointers.
translations.intro: Levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone when the body does not make enough of it. Taking it regularly, under consistent conditions, helps keep the treatment stable.

sections.heading: Keep a regular routine
sections.body: Follow your prescription and your medicine’s leaflet. Levothyroxine is usually taken on an empty stomach with water, leaving the recommended gap before breakfast. Coffee, tea and meals can also affect absorption: if your morning routine changes or becomes hard to stick to, ask for advice before changing how you take it.

sections.heading: Be careful with some products
sections.body: Iron, calcium and some antacids can reduce absorption if taken too close to levothyroxine. The gap to leave depends on the product: ask your pharmacist or doctor for advice.

sections.heading: If you miss a dose or something changes
sections.body: Do not double a dose on your own initiative. Ask your pharmacist or doctor what to do based on your prescription and when the dose was missed. Report any change of brand or in how you take it.

takeaways: Follow the leaflet and the instructions given by your healthcare professional.
Keep the conditions in which you take it as consistent as possible.
If in doubt, ask for advice rather than changing the dose yourself.

translations.title: Iron, calcium, magnesium: watch out for interactions
translations.summary: Some supplements can interfere with the absorption of levothyroxine when taken too close to it.
translations.intro: Dietary supplements and some medicines can change how levothyroxine is absorbed. This does not mean they are all forbidden, but spacing them out and professional advice matter.

sections.heading: Which products should you mention?
sections.body: Mention in particular supplements containing iron or calcium, some antacids and any new medicine. Formulations vary, and magnesium may also be present in some of the products concerned.

sections.heading: How long a gap should you leave?
sections.body: The gap depends on the product and its leaflet. Do not rely on a single rule for every supplement: check the leaflet and ask your pharmacist to confirm the right spacing.

sections.heading: An easy routine to follow
sections.body: Note the times you take each product in your routine and mention any change at your next appointment. Do not stop a prescribed treatment without medical advice.

takeaways: Tell your doctor or pharmacist about your medicines and supplements.
Check the exact gap in each product’s leaflet.
Do not adjust your levothyroxine dose without medical advice.

translations.title: Can some medicines affect the thyroid?
translations.summary: Some treatments can affect how the thyroid works or how it is monitored: always tell your care team about your medicines.
translations.intro: Some medicines can change how the thyroid works, or lead your doctor to plan regular checks. This does not mean you should stop the treatment: any decision is made with the professional who prescribes it.

sections.heading: Which treatments to mention
sections.body: Lithium and amiodarone are among the medicines that can affect the thyroid. Other treatments may also matter depending on your situation. Give your doctor and pharmacist an up-to-date list of your medicines, including those you take only now and then.

sections.heading: Why monitoring may be offered
sections.body: Your doctor considers the treatment, your medical history and your symptoms to decide whether thyroid blood tests or a check-up are useful. How often depends on the medicine and your situation.

sections.heading: Do not change a treatment yourself
sections.body: Do not stop a prescribed medicine or change its dose based on a guide or a single result. If you notice a change in your health or have a question about your treatment, contact the prescriber or your pharmacist.

takeaways: Some medicines can affect how the thyroid works.
Tell the professional who follows you about your treatments and medical history.
Do not stop or change a treatment without medical advice.

translations.title: Tiredness, sleep, mood: are they related?
translations.summary: These symptoms are common but can have several causes. Learn how to describe and track them.
translations.intro: Living with a thyroid condition can be draining, especially when energy or concentration fluctuate. How you feel deserves to be heard, even when it cannot be explained by a single factor.

sections.heading: Several causes are possible
sections.body: Tiredness may be linked to the thyroid, sleep, stress, another medical condition, a medicine or several factors combined. A tracking log cannot determine the cause on its own.

sections.heading: Observe without judging yourself
sections.body: For a few weeks, note your energy, your sleep, notable symptoms and recent changes. Look for trends rather than treating each bad day as a failure.

sections.heading: When should you bring it up?
sections.body: If symptoms persist, get worse or disrupt your daily life, book an appointment to discuss them. If you have significant or sudden difficulty breathing, seek urgent medical help.

takeaways: A symptom can have several causes.
Keeping a regular log helps prepare a medical discussion.
Do not adjust your treatment based on your symptoms alone.

translations.title: Preparing for a useful appointment
translations.summary: A few notes beforehand can help you talk about what really matters to you.
translations.intro: An appointment is a chance to review your results, symptoms and treatment. Preparing a few things can help make the conversation clearer.

sections.heading: Before the appointment
sections.body: Write down your main questions, the symptoms that bother you most and how they have changed, as well as any changes in medicines or supplements.

sections.heading: Bring the right information
sections.body: If possible, gather your latest results with their dates, the list of your treatments and any side effects you have noticed. Do not interpret the figures on your own: ask what they mean for you.

sections.heading: At the end of the appointment
sections.body: Go over the next steps in your own words: any tests, the follow-up schedule, how to take your treatment and who to contact if you have a question.

takeaways: Prepare three priority questions.
Bring dated results and the list of your treatments.
Leave with next steps you understand.

translations.title: Why check TSH after a change?
translations.summary: Lab follow-up is planned over time: the right moment depends on your situation and your prescription.
translations.intro: After a change in treatment, the body needs time to reach a new balance. The schedule of checks is set by your healthcare professional according to your situation.

sections.heading: Avoid drawing conclusions too quickly
sections.body: A test done too early may not reflect the balance reached after the change. Stick to the test date shown on your prescription.

sections.heading: Keep a record of changes
sections.body: Note the date of the change, the prescribed dose and the date of the next check. Tell your doctor about any new or unusual symptoms.

sections.heading: Do not adjust on your own
sections.body: Do not change the dose based on a single result or on a target found online. Your lab target and follow-up are tailored to you.

takeaways: Follow the prescribed schedule for tests.
Note dose changes and their dates.
Any change to your treatment must be discussed with the professional who follows you.

translations.title: Diet and the thyroid: sorting out the myths
translations.summary: No miracle food replaces medical follow-up. Be wary of restrictions and supplements presented as essential.
translations.intro: Diet contributes to overall health, but advice about the thyroid often circulates without taking individual needs or treatments into account.

sections.heading: No one-size-fits-all diet
sections.body: There is no single diet suited to everyone with Hashimoto’s. Cutting out foods or following a restrictive diet should not be undertaken without a clear reason and appropriate advice.

sections.heading: Supplements are not harmless
sections.body: A supplement may be useless, interact with a treatment or provide too much of a nutrient. Iodine, in particular, should not be taken in high doses without professional advice.

sections.heading: Focus on lasting habits
sections.body: Favour a varied diet and habits that suit your health and your daily life. For a specific question, talk to your doctor or a qualified dietitian.

takeaways: Be wary of promises of a cure and miracle solutions.
Do not start a high-dose supplement without professional advice.
Favour personalised advice over blanket bans.

sources.label: ANSES (French food safety agency) — Dietary supplements (in French)

translations.title: Planning a pregnancy or pregnant: talking about thyroid follow-up
translations.summary: Planning a pregnancy, or being pregnant, can change your thyroid follow-up: plan ahead to talk with your doctor or endocrinologist.
translations.intro: The body’s needs change during pregnancy, and thyroid follow-up may need to be adjusted. If you have a thyroid condition or take a treatment, tell your care team as soon as you are thinking about a pregnancy or find out that you are pregnant.

sections.heading: Prepare the conversation
sections.body: Share your diagnosis, your treatments, your latest results and any recent change. Do not wait for a routine appointment to tell your care team you are pregnant.

sections.heading: Follow-up suited to your situation
sections.body: Your doctor decides which tests are needed and how often, depending on your diagnosis, the stage of pregnancy and your treatment. Reference ranges may differ from those used outside pregnancy.

sections.heading: Do not change your treatment yourself
sections.body: Do not start, stop or change a medicine based on this guide. Ask for personal instructions, including for the period after the birth.

takeaways: Tell your care team if you are planning a pregnancy or are pregnant.
How often you are tested, and the targets, are set for you individually.
Ask for clear instructions before any change to your treatment.

translations.title: Can the thyroid change after giving birth?
translations.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis can temporarily change how the thyroid works, and it can go unnoticed.
translations.intro: In the months after giving birth, the way the thyroid works can change. Some symptoms can be mistaken for tiredness or the upheaval of life with a new baby. This guide gives general pointers; only a professional can assess your situation.

sections.heading: What is postpartum thyroiditis?
sections.body: It is an autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid that can appear after a pregnancy. How it evolves varies: some people go through a phase of hyperthyroidism, of hypothyroidism, or one after the other; others have few symptoms.

sections.heading: Which signs are worth discussing?
sections.body: Unusual tiredness, palpitations, feeling on edge or feeling slowed down can have many causes after a birth. If they persist, worry you or get worse, talk to a healthcare professional rather than deciding yourself that your thyroid is the cause.

sections.heading: How to raise it with your care team
sections.body: Mention any thyroid history, your treatments, the date of the birth and the changes you have noticed. The professional will decide whether a test or follow-up is useful. Do not stop a treatment without medical advice.

takeaways: How the thyroid works can change after a pregnancy.
Postpartum symptoms alone cannot tell you their cause.
A professional can decide whether tests are needed.

translations.title: Subacute thyroiditis: an inflammation that is often temporary
translations.summary: Some types of thyroid inflammation change over time; symptoms alone are not enough to work out the cause.
translations.intro: Thyroiditis means inflammation of the thyroid gland. Some types, such as subacute thyroiditis (also called de Quervain’s thyroiditis), can temporarily change thyroid hormone levels. Diagnosis and follow-up require a medical assessment.

sections.heading: It can evolve in several phases
sections.body: The inflammation may first come with signs of an overactive thyroid, followed by a period of underactivity before things improve. This pattern is not the same for everyone and cannot be confirmed from symptoms alone.

sections.heading: What to tell your doctor
sections.body: Tell your doctor about any pain or tenderness in your neck, a recent infection, palpitations, fever or other symptoms. These signs can have several causes and need to be interpreted in context.

sections.heading: Why follow-up may be offered
sections.body: Depending on the clinical assessment, your doctor may request blood tests or other investigations. Check-ups help follow how thyroid function changes. Do not start or stop a treatment without medical advice.

takeaways: Not all types of thyroiditis have the same cause or course.
Neck pain or other symptoms are not enough to make a diagnosis.
Your doctor decides which tests and follow-up are useful.

translations.title: Thyroid nodule: what does finding one mean?
translations.summary: A nodule is a localised lump in the thyroid. Finding one sometimes leads to further tests, but it does not, on its own, mean cancer.
translations.intro: A thyroid nodule may be found when a doctor examines your neck, or during a scan done for another reason. How it is assessed depends on several things, including how it looks on ultrasound and how well the thyroid is working. Only the professional who knows your situation can explain which tests are useful.

sections.heading: What is a nodule?
sections.body: It is a localised change in the structure of the gland. There may be one nodule or several. Finding a nodule does not, on its own, tell you what kind it is.

sections.heading: What tests may be offered?
sections.body: Your doctor may request a TSH blood test and an ultrasound scan. Depending on the results, they may suggest monitoring, a specialist opinion or a further test such as a fine-needle aspiration. Not every nodule needs the same tests.

sections.heading: What information to bring
sections.body: Bring any results you already have, scan reports, a list of your treatments and your questions. Tell your doctor about any recent change or discomfort in your neck.

takeaways: Finding a nodule does not tell you what kind it is.
The assessment depends on the examination, blood tests and ultrasound.
Your doctor will explain whether monitoring or a further test is appropriate.

translations.title: Thyroid ultrasound: what is it for?
translations.summary: An ultrasound scan shows the structure of the thyroid and can help describe a nodule or a goitre.
translations.intro: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves to look at the thyroid and nearby structures. It does not measure how much hormone the gland makes. A doctor requests it when it can answer a specific question; it is not needed for every thyroid condition.

sections.heading: What the scan can show
sections.body: The scan describes, among other things, the size and appearance of the gland, any nodules and some lymph nodes in the neck. The report gathers findings that will be interpreted alongside your situation and other tests.

sections.heading: What happens at the appointment
sections.body: A small probe is moved over the skin of your neck, usually with some gel. It is painless and does not use X-rays. Follow the instructions given by the imaging centre.

sections.heading: After the scan
sections.body: The report is not always a diagnosis on its own. Ask the doctor who requested it what the findings change for your follow-up and whether other tests are useful.

takeaways: Ultrasound looks at the structure of the thyroid, not at how much hormone it makes.
Whether you need one depends on the medical reason.
The report is read together with the rest of your medical file.

translations.title: Iodine contrast: what to mention before a scan
translations.summary: Some scans use an iodine-based contrast agent: mention any thyroid history and follow the team’s instructions.
translations.intro: Some imaging tests, such as CT scans, may use a contrast agent that contains iodine. If you have a thyroid condition or take a thyroid-related treatment, tell the medical team before the scan.

sections.heading: Why ask?
sections.body: A large amount of iodine can affect how the thyroid works in some people. The risk depends on your medical situation; it does not mean a scan with contrast is ruled out.

sections.heading: What to tell the team
sections.body: Mention any history of thyroid disease, your treatments and, if the team asks, any recent tests. If you are not sure whether contrast is planned, ask the imaging centre or the doctor who requested the scan.

sections.heading: Do not change the appointment yourself
sections.body: Do not refuse or postpone a scan based on this guide. The team will weigh the benefits, any precautions and whether follow-up is needed in your situation.

takeaways: Tell the team about a thyroid condition and its treatment.
Iodine in a contrast agent does not mean the scan must be cancelled.
Any precautions are decided by the medical team.

sources.label: American Thyroid Association — Potential risks of excess iodine

translations.title: What is Graves’ disease?
translations.summary: Understanding an autoimmune disease that can cause hyperthyroidism.
translations.intro: Graves’ disease (also called Basedow’s disease) is an autoimmune disease. The immune system produces antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor and can push the thyroid to make too much hormone.

sections.heading: What happens in the body?
sections.body: Stimulation of the thyroid can lead to hyperthyroidism. The signs and how intense they are vary from person to person.

sections.heading: What signs can appear?
sections.body: Palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, sweating, nervousness, tiredness, more frequent bowel movements or weight loss may occur. These signs are not enough on their own to make a diagnosis.

sections.heading: How is the diagnosis investigated?
sections.body: The doctor relies on symptoms, a clinical examination and blood tests, including TSH and thyroid hormones. TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) can help confirm Graves’ disease.

takeaways: Graves’ disease is autoimmune, but not all hyperthyroidism is caused by Graves’ disease.
Symptoms and results must be interpreted together.
Follow-up and treatment are tailored with your medical team.

translations.title: Graves’ disease and Hashimoto’s: what are the differences?
translations.summary: Two autoimmune diseases that can affect the thyroid in different ways.
translations.intro: Graves’ disease and Hashimoto’s are two autoimmune thyroid diseases. They are not interchangeable and may evolve differently.

sections.heading: Graves’ disease
sections.body: Antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor can lead to excessive production of thyroid hormones: hyperthyroidism.

sections.heading: Hashimoto’s
sections.body: Autoimmune inflammation can gradually reduce the thyroid’s ability to produce enough hormones, leading to hypothyroidism. Variations exist and the medical context matters.

sections.heading: Why does this distinction matter?
sections.body: Tests, treatments and monitoring depend on the cause and on hormone levels. Only a professional can interpret an individual situation.

takeaways: Both diseases involve the immune system.
Graves’ disease is often associated with hyperthyroidism; Hashimoto’s with hypothyroidism.
The disease should not be inferred from a single symptom or a single lab value.

translations.title: What are TRAb antibodies for?
translations.summary: An important lab marker when investigating Graves’ disease.
translations.intro: TRAb are antibodies directed against the TSH receptor. Some can stimulate this receptor and contribute to the hyperthyroidism of Graves’ disease.

sections.heading: Why measure them?
sections.body: In a suggestive context, the test can help the doctor identify the cause of hyperthyroidism and contribute to follow-up depending on the situation.

sections.heading: Is a positive result enough?
sections.body: No: it is interpreted alongside symptoms, the clinical examination, TSH, thyroid hormones and the laboratory’s methods.

sections.heading: What if the result is negative?
sections.body: A negative result should not be interpreted on its own to rule out every possible cause. The doctor decides whether other tests are useful.

takeaways: TRAb stands for TSH receptor antibodies.
The result is read together with the rest of your tests.
Ask your healthcare professional what this result actually changes for your follow-up.

translations.title: Recognising the possible signs of hyperthyroidism
translations.summary: Symptoms can affect the body, sleep and mood.
translations.intro: When the thyroid produces too much hormone, several body functions can speed up. The signs vary and can have other causes.

sections.heading: Possible physical signs
sections.body: Palpitations, tremor, feeling unusually hot, sweating, unintended weight loss or more frequent bowel movements may appear.

sections.heading: Energy and mood
sections.body: Some people feel nervous, irritable, anxious or have trouble sleeping, while also feeling very tired.

sections.heading: What to log in ThyroTrack?
sections.body: Note the date, the symptoms, how intense they are, the circumstances and any recent changes. These observations can help you prepare for an appointment, without replacing a medical assessment.

takeaways: A single symptom is not enough to diagnose hyperthyroidism.
New, persistent or worsening symptoms deserve medical advice.
Chest pain, feeling seriously unwell or severe shortness of breath call for urgent care.

translations.title: Graves’ disease and the eyes: which signs to watch for?
translations.summary: Thyroid eye disease deserves particular attention.
translations.intro: Graves’ disease can be associated with inflammation of the tissues around the eyes, known as thyroid eye disease (Graves’ orbitopathy). It does not affect everyone with the disease.

sections.heading: What signs can appear?
sections.body: Dryness, a gritty feeling, redness, swollen eyelids, more prominent eyes or double vision may occur.

sections.heading: When should you seek advice?
sections.body: Report any new eye symptom to a healthcare professional promptly. Reduced vision, a change in how you see colours or significant eye pain needs urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Why report it?
sections.body: Follow-up may require coordination between the doctor who manages your thyroid and an ophthalmologist.

sections.heading: Smoking: talking about it without judgement
sections.body: Smoking, including exposure to other people’s smoke, is linked to thyroid eye disease being more common or more severe in Graves’ disease. This does not mean that everyone who smokes will develop it. If you would like to cut down or stop smoking, a healthcare professional can offer support suited to you.

takeaways: Eye symptoms should be reported.
Do not assume that a vision problem is necessarily caused by Graves’ disease.
Sudden or significant loss of vision is an emergency.
You can ask for support to cut down or stop smoking, without judgement.

sources.label: American Thyroid Association — Thyroid eye disease

translations.title: Understanding antithyroid medicines
translations.summary: What are they for, and why does follow-up matter?
translations.intro: Antithyroid medicines, prescribed in some cases of hyperthyroidism, reduce the production of thyroid hormones. The choice and length of treatment depend on the individual situation.

sections.heading: Follow-up is necessary
sections.body: Blood tests and appointments allow your healthcare professional to monitor how things are going and adjust your care.

sections.heading: Fever or sore throat during treatment
sections.body: Some antithyroid medicines can, rarely, cause a sharp drop in white blood cells. If you have a fever, a sore throat or signs of infection during treatment, seek medical advice immediately, the same day, to find out what to do. Do not make treatment decisions based on this guide alone.

sections.heading: Other unusual signs
sections.body: Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine or significant abdominal pain also need prompt medical advice.

takeaways: Follow your prescription and the prescribed follow-up.
Keep your medical team’s contact details close at hand.
This guide does not replace your prescriber’s personalised instructions.

translations.title: Radioactive iodine: how the treatment works
translations.summary: Radioactive iodine is an option in some cases of hyperthyroidism, with precautions and follow-up set by a specialist team.
translations.intro: Radioactive iodine (radioiodine) treatment may be offered for some causes of hyperthyroidism. The decision depends on the condition, the other possible treatments and your situation. The treatment is organised by a specialist team.

sections.heading: How does it work?
sections.body: The thyroid takes up iodine. The treatment aims to reduce the activity of some of the thyroid cells. It does not work straight away, and the result varies from one situation to another.

sections.heading: What precautions should you ask about?
sections.body: Whether it suits you, the reasons it might not, and the radiation safety advice should all be explained by the nuclear medicine team. Tell them if you could be pregnant, are breastfeeding or are planning a pregnancy, and about all your treatments, before the treatment is arranged.

sections.heading: Why does follow-up continue?
sections.body: How the thyroid works can change after treatment. Check-ups are planned, and thyroid hormone replacement may become necessary if the thyroid no longer makes enough hormones. Do not stop or change a treatment without medical advice.

takeaways: Radioactive iodine is not suitable for every thyroid condition.
Precautions are personal and should come from the specialist team.
Blood tests are still needed after treatment.

translations.title: Remission and relapse: understanding Graves’ disease follow-up
translations.summary: The course of the disease varies from person to person and calls for tailored follow-up.
translations.intro: After treatment, some people experience lasting remission, while others may have a relapse. How things will evolve cannot be predicted from a single result.

sections.heading: What is remission?
sections.body: The term refers to a period during which the disease is controlled, without clinical or lab signs of hyperthyroidism, according to the criteria used by the medical team.

sections.heading: Why continue follow-up?
sections.body: Things can change over time. The doctor sets how often appointments and tests take place, including after a supervised change or stop of treatment.

sections.heading: What can you do?
sections.body: Keep a record of results, treatments and symptoms. Do not stop or change a treatment without medical instructions.

takeaways: The journey varies from person to person.
Follow-up remains important even when you feel better.
If symptoms come back, contact your healthcare professional.

translations.title: TSH, FT4 and FT3: understanding hyperthyroidism tests
translations.summary: Results are understood together, never in isolation.
translations.intro: TSH is a regulating signal produced by the pituitary gland. Free T4 and free T3 are thyroid hormones measured in some situations to clarify hormone status.

sections.heading: A commonly seen pattern
sections.body: In overt hyperthyroidism, TSH is often low and FT4 and/or FT3 are high. However, there are special situations and limits to interpretation.

sections.heading: Why context matters
sections.body: Results depend in particular on symptoms, treatments, medical history, when the sample was taken and the laboratory’s reference ranges.

sections.heading: How to prepare your questions
sections.body: Ask your doctor what the results mean in your case, whether other tests are needed and when the next check is planned.

takeaways: Avoid comparing results without looking at the laboratory’s units and reference ranges.
A single value is not enough to identify the cause.
Do not change your treatment based on a guide or a single result.

translations.title: Preparing your appointment when you have Graves’ disease
translations.summary: A few simple notes to make the appointment more useful.
translations.intro: Preparing some information in advance can help explain what has changed since your last appointment.

sections.heading: What to gather
sections.body: Your recent results, the list of your medicines and prescribed doses, the dates of any changes and any side effects.

sections.heading: What to note
sections.body: Your symptoms, how often they occur, how intense they are, difficulties in daily life and the questions you would like to raise.

sections.heading: What to ask
sections.body: What is the follow-up plan? When should the tests be repeated? Which signs mean you should call promptly? Who should you contact if there is a problem with your treatment?

takeaways: Bring your results with their dates and reference ranges.
Report any new symptom, especially affecting the eyes or the heart.
Ask for clear instructions for unexpected situations.

translations.title: After thyroid surgery: understanding your follow-up
translations.summary: After thyroid surgery, follow-up depends on the operation and why it was done; your team explains the treatment and check-ups you need.
translations.intro: An operation can remove part or all of the thyroid. Recovery and follow-up depend on the operation, the reason for it and the results. Your care team will give you instructions suited to your situation.

sections.heading: Hormone treatment after surgery
sections.body: After the whole thyroid is removed, thyroid hormone replacement is usually needed. After a partial operation, it depends on how much hormone the remaining thyroid makes and on your follow-up results.

sections.heading: Check-ups and symptoms to report
sections.body: The schedule of appointments and blood tests is set for you individually. Follow your discharge instructions and contact the team about any symptom that worries you. Severe or worsening difficulty breathing needs urgent help.

sections.heading: Getting ready to go home
sections.body: Before you leave hospital, check who to contact, when to restart your medicines, which appointments are planned and which activities to avoid for now. Ask for an explanation if an instruction is unclear.

takeaways: Recovery depends on the type of operation and the reason for it.
Hormone treatment is not the same for everyone.
Keep your discharge instructions and your team’s contact details.

translations.title: When is difficulty breathing an emergency?
translations.summary: Do not wait for a guide or an appointment if breathing becomes difficult.
translations.intro: Significant, sudden or worsening difficulty breathing should not automatically be put down to the thyroid or to anxiety.

sections.heading: What should you do?
sections.body: If you have significant difficulty breathing, are choking, have rapid swelling of the neck with breathing difficulty, chest pain or feel seriously unwell, call the emergency services: 112 in the European Union (or 15 in France). Elsewhere, use your local emergency number.

sections.heading: Do not wait
sections.body: Do not rely on an information guide to decide whether a serious symptom can wait. Seek urgent help.

takeaways: Significant breathing difficulties are an emergency.
An educational guide cannot assess severity remotely.
If in doubt about significant breathing difficulty, seek help immediately.
